title: PGM: Practical Growth Modeling for jamovi
text:
0.1 Scope
PGM — Practical Growth Modeling is a jamovi module for fitting, evaluating, and interpreting nonlinear biological growth curves.
The module implements the Unified family of sigmoidal growth models and provides tools for:
PGM is intended for researchers analyzing longitudinal or cross-sectional growth data in animal science, plant science, microbiology, ecology, developmental biology, and related fields.
The documentation is divided into four main parts:

title: PGM: Practical Growth Modeling for jamovi
PGM: Practical Growth Modeling for jamovi
text:
0.2 Important considerations
PGM assists with model specification, estimation, and interpretation but does not replace statistical judgment.
Model selection should not be based on a single goodness-of-fit statistic. The adequacy of the mean function, fixed-effects structure, random-effects structure, residual variance, residual dependence, parameter plausibility, data coverage, and residual diagnostics should be considered jointly.
Complex fixed-effect interactions and random-effects structures also require adequate replication. PGM checks several basic estimability conditions, but a model that converges is not necessarily scientifically appropriate.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1 Why use parametric growth models?
Growth is a dynamic process in which the size, mass, concentration, or other measurable characteristic of a biological system changes over time.
Sigmoidal growth models summarize an entire trajectory using a small number of parameters related to characteristics such as:
PGM provides a graphical interface for fitting these models in jamovi, while retaining statistical procedures commonly implemented in R.
Parametric growth models can provide interpretable summaries of nonlinear trajectories. Depending on the selected model, their parameters may describe:
These interpretations depend on the equation and parametrization used. Parameters with similar names are not necessarily equivalent across different growth models.

3  Installation
text:
3.1 Installing jamovi
PGM is an add-on module for jamovi. Before installing the module, download and install the current version of jamovi from its official website.
After installation, open jamovi and verify that the main analysis interface is working correctly.

title: 3  Installation
section: 3.2 Installing PGM from the jamovi library
text:
3.2 Installing PGM from the jamovi library
PGM is available in the official jamovi library:

Open jamovi.
Select the Modules icon, in the upper-right of Analysis menu.
Open the jamovi module library.
Search for PGM.
Select Install.

After installation, “Growth” option will appear in the main analysis ribbon.

title: 3  Installation
text:
3.3 Installing a development version
Development versions may be distributed as .jmo files on PGM GitHub repository.

To install a local module:
Open jamovi.
Select the Modules icon.
Select Sideload.
Locate the .jmo file.
Confirm the installation.

Development versions may contain recently added features that have not yet been included in a stable release.

title: 3  Installation
text:
3.4 Updating PGM
When PGM is installed through the jamovi library, available updates can be installed through the module manager.
For reproducible academic work, record the PGM and jamovi versions.

title: 3  Installation
text:
3.5 Verifying the installation
After installation, open a dataset containing numeric time and response variables. The module includes example datasets for testing and learning purposes. They are available from the jamovi menu in the upper-left corner: Open → Data Library → PGM.
Next, select Growth from the analysis ribbon and open Curve Modeling. Assign at least one response variable and one time variable.
If the analysis interface opens and produces an initial result, the module has been installed successfully.

title: 4  Data preparation
text:
4.5 Variable requirements

4.5.1 Response
The response must be numeric and should represent a process compatible with the selected growth equation.
Examples include body mass, length, concentration, plant height, biomass, or cumulative production.


4.5.2 Time
Time must be numeric.
Examples include:

age in days;
age in weeks;
hours after inoculation;
days after planting.

The unit of time determines the numerical scale of time-dependent model parameters and derivative quantities.


4.5.3 Fixed-effect predictors
Fixed effects represent systematic changes in one or more growth parameters.
Predictors may be categorical or continuous.
Categorical predictors must contain at least two observed levels in the data actually used for the fit. Interaction terms also require sufficient observations in the relevant combinations of predictor levels.
For each growth parameter, the selected fixed-effect terms define a separate parameter model.
For example,
\[
\log(K)
=
\beta_0+
\beta_1 X+
\beta_2 Z+
\beta_3 XZ
\]
represents main effects of \(X\) and \(Z\) and their interaction on the internally estimated \(K\) parameter.


4.5.4 Random-effects grouping variables
Random-effects grouping variables identify units among which one or more growth parameters are allowed to vary.
Examples include:

subject;
animal;
nest;
batch;
experimental unit.

Several grouping levels may be used when they form a nested hierarchy.
For example, using the Imperial Shag dataset included with PGM (Svagelj et al. 2021):
nestID
chickID
may represent chicks nested within nests when each chick belongs to one nest.
Composite grouping terms may also be created explicitly. A term such as
species:replicate
represents the unique combinations of species and replicate.
The current implementation requires a unique nested hierarchy. Crossed random-effects structures that cannot be represented as a unique nesting order are not supported.


4.5.5 Correlation Groups
Correlation Groups define the units within which an AR(1) or CAR(1) residual correlation structure is applied.
When more than one variable is selected, they define an ordered grouping hierarchy from outer to inner level.
For example:
nestID / chickID
models residual correlation within chicks nested in nests.
Correlation Groups are conceptually distinct from random effects. They may coincide with random-effects groups, but they serve a different statistical purpose.

title: 4  Data preparation
4  Data preparation
text:
4.7 Factor levels and estimability
Unused factor levels are removed before GNLS or NLME estimation.
PGM checks whether categorical fixed-effect predictors retain at least two observed levels and whether the resulting fixed-effects design matrix has full column rank.
Empty combinations of factor levels, redundant terms, or perfect collinearity may make a requested effect or interaction non-estimable.

title: 4  Data preparation
text:
4.8 Measurement schedule
Discrete AR(1) correlation is most naturally used when observations follow an approximately equally spaced measurement schedule.
For irregularly spaced measurements, continuous-time CAR(1) is generally more appropriate because correlation is modeled using the actual temporal distance.

text:
5.1 Opening the analysis
To begin:
A model setup defines the response variable, growth model, residual variance structure, residual correlation structure, and optional fixed asymptote.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
Open the dataset in jamovi.
Select PGM from the analysis ribbon.
Open Growth Curve Modeling.
Assign one or more Dependent Variables.
Assign the numeric Time Variable.
Configure one or more rows in Model Setup.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
5.2 Model parameterization
PGM provides two location parameterizations for the Unified growth-model family.

5.2.1 Ti
The Ti parameterization reports the time of the inflection point.
This form is useful when the timing of maximum growth rate has a direct biological interpretation.


5.2.2 W0
The W0 parameterization reports the fitted response at \(t=0\).
This form may be useful when the initial value has a direct biological interpretation or when comparison at a common temporal origin is important.
The parameterization is selected globally for the analysis and the corresponding parameter label is updated in the Fixed Effects and Random Effects sections.

title: 5  Running an analysis
5  Running an analysis
text:
5.4 Fixed asymptote
A positive value may be entered in the Asymptote column of a Model Setup.
When supplied, \(A\) is treated as fixed rather than estimated for that setup.
This may be useful when the upper asymptote is externally known or when incomplete late-stage data make free asymptote estimation scientifically inappropriate.
Because \(A\) is then not an estimated parameter, fixed or random effects assigned to \(A\) are not fitted for that setup.

title: 5  Running an analysis
5  Running an analysis
text:
5.6 Residual correlation
The Correlation column controls residual serial dependence.
Available options are:

None;
AR(1);
CAR(1).

When AR(1) or CAR(1) is selected, one or more variables must be assigned under Correlation Groups.
AR(1) is most appropriate for approximately equally spaced repeated observations.
CAR(1) uses the actual temporal distance and is generally preferable for irregularly spaced observations.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
5.7 Fixed Effects
The Fixed Effects section assigns predictors to individual growth parameters.
For example, the terms
sex
treatment
sex:treatment
assigned to \(A\) specify:
\[
\log(A)
=
\beta_0+
\beta_1\,sex+
\beta_2\,treatment+
\beta_3\,sex\times treatment.
\]
The exact internal parameter scale depends on the selected growth parameter.
Main effects and interaction terms are specified explicitly. An interaction does not replace its component main effects unless that is the intended model.
The same fixed-effect specification is applied to each model setup in which the corresponding structural parameter is estimated.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
5.8 Random Effects
The Random Effects section assigns grouping terms to individual growth parameters.
For example, the Imperial Shag dataset distributed with PGM contains chick and nest identifiers (Svagelj et al. 2021):
A: chickID
allows the asymptotic parameter to vary among chicks.
Different growth parameters may receive different random grouping structures.
Multiple nested levels are also supported. For example:
nestID
chickID
may represent chicks nested within nests when the data support that hierarchy.
A composite term such as
species:replicate
creates a grouping factor from the unique combinations of its components.
Random-effect interaction terms therefore describe combined grouping units; they are not fixed-effect interactions and are not random slopes for predictor variables.
Within each grouping level, PGM currently uses a diagonal covariance structure for multiple random growth parameters.

title: 5  Running an analysis
text:
5.9 Correlation Groups
Correlation Groups define the grouping hierarchy for residual autocorrelation.
For example:
nestID
chickID
corresponds to an outer-to-inner hierarchy equivalent to nestID/chickID.
When random effects are also present, PGM reconciles their hierarchy with the selected correlation groups and stops with an informative error if the structures are incompatible.

6  Overview
text:
6.1 Estimation pathways
PGM selects the final estimation framework according to the requested fixed effects, random effects, residual variance function, and residual correlation structure.
All pathways begin with an initial nonlinear fit using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm (Elzhov et al. 2023).
The initial fit provides starting values for the more general GNLS or NLME specification when these are required.

title: 6  Overview
6  Overview
text:
6.3 Fixed effects
Fixed effects represent systematic changes in growth parameters.
Each estimated structural parameter has its own fixed-effects formula.
Categorical predictors, continuous predictors, and interaction terms are supported.
When no fixed effects are assigned to a parameter, that parameter is represented by an intercept-only model.

title: 6  Overview
text:
6.4 Random effects
Random effects represent persistent differences in growth parameters among grouping units.
Random grouping terms are assigned separately to the structural parameters.
When at least one random effect is specified, PGM fits the model using nlme with maximum likelihood (Pinheiro et al. 2026).
The current implementation uses diagonal covariance matrices within each random grouping level.

title: 6  Overview
6  Overview
text:
6.6 Residual correlation
Residual serial dependence may be represented using:

discrete AR(1);
continuous-time CAR(1).

Correlation Groups define the hierarchy within which residual correlation is evaluated.
Residual correlation may be used with GNLS or NLME models.

title: 6  Overview
section: 6.7 Mean, random, variance, and correlation components

title: 6  Overview
text:
6.8 Maximum likelihood
Nonlinear mixed-effects models in PGM are estimated using maximum likelihood.
Likelihood-based comparisons should only be made between models fitted to the same response observations and under compatible likelihood definitions.

Pinheiro, José, Douglas Bates, and R Core Team. 2026. nlme: Linear and Nonlinear Mixed Effects Models. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.nlme.

title: 7  Growth Models
text:
7.1 Unified growth-model family
PGM implements the Unified family of sigmoidal growth models described by Tjørve and Tjørve (Tjørve and Tjørve 2010; Tjørve and Tjørve 2017).
The implemented family contains:
The common parameters retain the same interpretation across family members.

title: 7  Growth Models
7  Growth Models
text:
7.2 Regularized Unified-Richards representation
PGM uses
\[
\lambda = \log(d),
\]
and defines
\[
a = e^\lambda - 1.
\]
For \(a\neq0\), define
\[
R(\lambda,x)
=
\exp\left[
-\frac{\log(1+ax)}{a}
\right].
\]
At the Gompertz limit, \(\lambda=0\) and \(a=0\), the continuous limit is
\[
R(0,x)=e^{-x}.
\]
The implementation evaluates this expression using numerically stable expm1() and log1p() formulations.
This avoids a singularity at \(d=1\) and allows the Richards surface to remain continuous through the Gompertz limit.

title: 7  Growth Models
text:
7.3 Shape parameter
For Unified Richards,
\[
d=e^\lambda>0
\]
is estimated freely.
The three-parameter family members correspond to fixed values of \(\lambda\):



Model
\(d\)
\(\lambda\)




Gompertz
\(1\)
\(0\)


Logistic
\(2\)
\(\log 2\)


von Bertalanffy
\(2/3\)
\(\log(2/3)\)



Only Richards estimates \(d\) from the data.

title: 7  Growth Models
7  Growth Models
text:
7.5 W0 parameterization
The alternative W0 form replaces \(T_i\) with the fitted response at the time origin:
\[
W_0=W(0).
\]
The Ti and W0 forms describe the same family of curve shapes; they differ only in the location parameter used to describe the trajectory.

title: 7  Growth Models
text:
7.6 Fixed asymptote
The asymptote may optionally be supplied as a fixed positive value.
When \(A\) is fixed, it is removed from the estimated parameter vector.
This can be useful when:

the asymptote is externally known;
biological constraints justify a predetermined value;
late-stage data are incomplete and unrestricted asymptote estimation is not desired.

Fixing the asymptote changes the statistical model and should therefore be scientifically justified.

title: 7  Growth Models
text:
7.7 Parameter transformations
For estimated parameters, PGM uses:
\[
A=\exp(\alpha),
\]
\[
K=\exp(\kappa),
\]
and, for Richards,
\[
d=\exp(\lambda).
\]
Under the W0 parameterization,
\[
\eta_0=
\operatorname{logit}\left(\frac{W_0}{A}\right).
\]
These transformations enforce the required parameter domains while allowing unconstrained numerical optimization on the transformed scales.

title: 7  Growth Models
text:
7.8 Starting values
Starting values are generated automatically from the observed trajectory.
PGM uses a smooth spline to obtain an initial approximation to the growth rate.
The initial asymptote is based on a value above the observed maximum unless a fixed asymptote is supplied. The initial location and growth-rate parameters are then derived from the smoothed trajectory and the selected Unified model.
Starting values are computational aids and should not be interpreted as model estimates.




Tjørve, Even, and Kathleen M. C. Tjørve. 2010. “A Unified Approach to the Richards-Model Family for Use in Growth Analyses: Why We Need Only Two Model Forms.” Journal of Theoretical Biology 267 (3): 417–25. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2010.09.008.


Tjørve, Kathleen M. C., and Even Tjørve. 2017. “A Proposed Family of Unified Models for Sigmoidal Growth.” Ecological Modelling 359: 117–27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2017.05.008.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.1 Initial nonlinear fit
PGM first fits the selected Unified growth equation using nonlinear least squares and the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm (Elzhov et al. 2023).
The initial fit serves two purposes:

title: 8  Estimation
text:
it provides the final estimates for an ordinary nonlinear model;
it provides starting values for GNLS or NLME estimation when additional model structures are requested.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.2 Final estimation framework
An ordinary NLS fit is retained when the model contains only the growth equation.
GNLS is used when no random effects are specified but the model contains one or more of:

fixed-effect predictors;
a residual variance function;
an AR(1) or CAR(1) residual correlation structure.

NLME is used whenever at least one growth parameter contains a random effect.
NLME models are estimated by maximum likelihood using the nlme framework (Pinheiro et al. 2026).

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.3 Parameter-specific fixed effects
Each estimated growth parameter has its own fixed-effects formula.
For example,
\[
\log(A)
=
\beta_{A0}
+
\beta_{A1}X
\]
and
\[
\log(K)
=
\beta_{K0}
+
\beta_{K1}Z
+
\beta_{K2}Q
+
\beta_{K3}ZQ
\]
may be fitted simultaneously.
A parameter with no assigned predictors is represented by an intercept-only formula.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.4 Parameter transformations
Positive parameters are fitted on transformed scales.
The principal internal transformations are:
\[
A=\exp(\alpha),
\]
\[
K=\exp(\kappa),
\]
\[
d=\exp(\lambda)
\]
for free Richards shape, and
\[
\eta_0=
\operatorname{logit}\left(\frac{W_0}{A}\right)
\]
under the W0 parameterization.
\(T_i\) is fitted directly on its natural time scale.
When the asymptote is fixed, \(A\) is removed from the estimated parameter vector.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.5 Fixed-effect design validation
Before GNLS or NLME estimation, PGM removes unused factor levels and checks the requested fixed-effects structure.
Categorical predictors must retain at least two observed levels.
The model matrix for each growth parameter must also have full column rank.
Empty factor combinations, redundant interactions, or perfectly collinear predictors therefore produce an informative error rather than an unidentified fit.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.6 Natural-scale parameter profiles
The model is fitted on its estimation scale, but the parameter table reports values on the natural growth-parameter scale.
For categorical predictors, the first observed factor level is used as the reference level.
For continuous predictors, the reference profile is evaluated at zero.
Rows corresponding to continuous effects represent the parameter profile at a predictor value of one relative to the zero reference profile.
For interactions, the reported natural-scale parameter value includes the associated main-effect and interaction contributions required by that predictor profile.

title: 8  Estimation
text:
8.7 Standard errors
The covariance matrix is obtained on the model estimation scale.
For a reported natural-scale quantity
\[
g(\boldsymbol\theta),
\]
PGM uses a first-order delta approximation:
\[
\operatorname{Var}
\left[
g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})
\right]
\approx
J
\operatorname{Var}
(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})
J^\mathsf{T},
\]
where \(J\) is the Jacobian of the transformation evaluated at the corresponding parameter profile.
For \(W_0\), uncertainty propagation includes its joint dependence on both the asymptote and the internal initial-value parameter when \(A\) is estimated.

title: 8  Estimation
8  Estimation
text:
8.9 Fixed-effect p-values
When fixed effects are present, PGM reports coefficient-level p-values obtained from the fitted NLS/GNLS/NLME model on the model estimation scale.
These are tests of individual model coefficients.
They are not automatically omnibus tests of an entire multi-level factor or interaction term.
For categorical predictors, coefficients are interpreted relative to the reference level.
For interactions, the reported p-value corresponds to the relevant interaction coefficient on the estimation scale.




Elzhov, Timur V., Katharine M. Mullen, Andrej-Nikolai Spiess, and Ben Bolker. 2023. minpack.lm: R Interface to the Levenberg-Marquardt Nonlinear Least-Squares Algorithm Found in MINPACK, Plus Support for Bounds. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.minpack.lm.


Pinheiro, José, Douglas Bates, and R Core Team. 2026. nlme: Linear and Nonlinear Mixed Effects Models. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.nlme.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.1 When mixed effects are used
PGM fits a nonlinear mixed-effects model whenever at least one random effect is assigned to a growth parameter (Pinheiro et al. 2026).
Random effects represent persistent variation in structural growth parameters among grouping units.
They are distinct from residual variation and residual autocorrelation.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.2 Parameter-specific random effects
Random effects may be assigned independently to the estimated growth parameters.
For example,
\[
\log(A_i)
=
\log(A)+b_{Ai}
\]
allows the asymptote to vary among subjects, whereas
\[
\log(K_i)
=
\log(K)+b_{Ki}
\]
allows the Unified growth-rate parameter to vary.
Under the Ti parameterization, \(T_i\) may also contain a random effect.
Under the W0 parameterization, the corresponding internal initial-value parameter may contain a random effect.
For Richards, the shape parameter \(d\) may also vary randomly.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.3 Different grouping structures by parameter
Different growth parameters may be assigned to different grouping levels.
For example, using grouping variables available in the Imperial Shag dataset of Svagelj et al. (Svagelj et al. 2021):

\(A\): nestID;
\(K\): chickID;
\(T_i\): chickID.

The resulting model allows different sources of between-unit variation to act on different aspects of the growth trajectory.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.4 Nested grouping structures
PGM supports multiple grouping levels when they form a unique nested hierarchy.
For example,
nestID
chickID
may be interpreted as chicks nested within nests when every chick belongs to exactly one nest.
The hierarchy is evaluated from the observed grouping structure and, when residual Correlation Groups are supplied, from their explicit order.
Grouping selections that form crossed or otherwise non-orderable structures are rejected.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.5 Composite grouping terms
The Random Effects interface also allows interaction terms between grouping variables.
For random effects, a term such as
species:replicate
does not represent a fixed-effect interaction.
It defines a new grouping factor whose levels are the unique combinations of species and replicate.
For example,
species
species:replicate
may represent replicate units nested within species.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.6 Random-effects covariance
Within each grouping level, PGM currently uses a diagonal random-effects covariance structure.
If more than one growth parameter varies at the same grouping level, their random deviations are therefore estimated with separate variances but without estimated covariance terms.
This is equivalent to using a pdDiag structure in nlme.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.7 Random-effects output
The Random Effects table reports:

grouping level;
growth parameter;
estimated standard deviation.

The reported SD is expressed on the natural growth-parameter scale.
For log-transformed parameters, PGM converts the fitted transformed-scale variation to the induced natural-scale variation.
For \(W_0\), a first-order delta approximation is used at the reference profile.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.8 Fixed and random effects together
A growth parameter may contain both fixed and random effects.
The fixed effects describe systematic population-level differences associated with predictors.
The random effects describe remaining persistent variation among grouping units around those systematic patterns.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.10 Conditional fitted values
Residual diagnostics for nonlinear mixed-effects models use conditional fitted values at the innermost random-effects grouping level.
Consequently, these diagnostics describe fit to the grouped trajectories after accounting for estimated random effects rather than only the population-average curve.

title: 9  Mixed Effects
text:
9.11 Current limitations
The current interface assumes a uniquely nested grouping hierarchy.
General crossed random-effects structures are not supported.
Random-effect interaction terms define composite grouping units; they do not define random slopes for fixed-effect predictors.




Pinheiro, José, Douglas Bates, and R Core Team. 2026. nlme: Linear and Nonlinear Mixed Effects Models. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.nlme.


Svagelj, Walter S., Agustina Gómez-Laich, María Rita Pérez, Gustavo M. Somoza, and Flavio Quintana. 2021. “Sex-Specific Environmental Sensitivity on the Postnatal Growth of a Sexually Size-Dimorphic Seabird.” Ibis 163 (3): 1032–44. https://doi.org/10.1111/ibi.12920.

title: 10  Variance Functions
text:
10.1 Power variance function
Ordinary nonlinear least squares assumes constant residual variance:
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2.\]
This assumption is often unrealistic for biological growth data because larger responses may exhibit greater absolute variability.
PGM provides alternative residual variance functions based on the fitted response \(\hat y_i\), implemented through the variance-function structures available in nlme (Pinheiro et al. 2026).
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)
=
\sigma^2 |\hat y_i|^{2\theta}.\]
Interpretation:

title: 10  Variance Functions
10  Variance Functions
text:
10.2 Exponential variance function
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)
=
\sigma^2 \exp(2\theta\hat y_i).\]
This model represents an exponential relationship between residual standard deviation and fitted response.

title: 10  Variance Functions
text:
10.3 Constant-plus-power variance function
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)
=
\sigma^2
\left(
\theta_1 + |\hat y_i|^{\theta_2}
\right)^2.\]
This structure permits a nonzero baseline component together with a power-related increase or decrease in residual variation.

title: 10  Variance Functions
11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.1 Correlation Groups
Repeated observations from the same experimental unit may remain correlated even after the mean structure and random effects have been modeled.
PGM provides first-order discrete and continuous-time residual correlation structures through the nlme framework (Pinheiro et al. 2026).
Residual correlation is defined within the variables selected under Correlation Groups.
When more than one grouping variable is supplied, their order defines an outer-to-inner hierarchy.
For example, using the grouping variables from the Imperial Shag example dataset (Svagelj et al. 2021):
nestID
chickID
corresponds to a correlation grouping structure conceptually equivalent to
\[
\text{nestID}/\text{chickID}.
\]
When AR(1) or CAR(1) is selected, at least one Correlation Group is required.
Correlation Groups are independent of the Random Effects specification, although the two structures must be mutually compatible when they are used together.

title: 11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.2 AR(1)
For observations separated by \(h\) discrete measurement lags,
\[
\operatorname{Corr}
(\varepsilon_{i,t},\varepsilon_{i,t+h})
=
\phi^{|h|},
\]
where
\[
-1<\phi<1.
\]
AR(1) is most naturally interpreted when observations are ordered and approximately equally spaced.
The model describes correlation by discrete measurement lag rather than by arbitrary continuous temporal distance.

title: 11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.3 CAR(1)
For observations made at times \(t_{ij}\) and \(t_{ik}\),
\[
\operatorname{Corr}
(\varepsilon_{ij},\varepsilon_{ik})
=
\phi^{|t_{ij}-t_{ik}|}.
\]
CAR(1) uses the actual temporal separation between observations and is therefore generally more appropriate for irregularly spaced measurements.

title: 11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.4 Correlation without random effects
Residual correlation does not require a random-effects model.
If AR(1) or CAR(1) is requested without random effects, PGM fits the structure through generalized nonlinear least squares.

title: 11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.5 Correlation with random effects
When random effects are present, PGM reconciles the random grouping hierarchy with the selected Correlation Groups.
A composite random grouping term may represent the same grouping unit as a sequence of correlation groups.
For example,
species:replicate
may be used as a random grouping unit while
species / replicate
defines the corresponding residual-correlation hierarchy.
The model is rejected when the random and correlation grouping structures cannot be represented by a compatible nested hierarchy.

title: 11  Residual Correlation
text:
11.6 Random effects are not autocorrelation
Random effects and residual correlation represent different dependence mechanisms.
A random effect represents persistent differences among growth trajectories.
Residual autocorrelation represents association between observation-level departures occurring close together in time.
A model may require one, both, or neither structure.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.1 Derivative notation
Let \(W(t)\) denote the fitted growth function.
PGM may calculate:
\[W'(t),\]
the instantaneous growth rate, and
\[W''(t),\]
the growth acceleration.
Higher-order derivatives are used for selected geometric descriptors.
These quantities are properties of the fitted curve and inherit any misspecification or uncertainty in the underlying growth model.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.2 Inflection point
The inflection point is identified from a sign change in the second derivative:
\[W''(t)=0.\]
At the inflection point of a standard sigmoidal trajectory, the growth rate is at its maximum.
When no sign change is found within the evaluated interval, PGM reports that no inflection point was detected.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.3 Acceleration extrema
Following Gregorczyk (1991), PGM defines:

\(P1\): time of maximum positive growth acceleration before the inflection point;
\(P2\): time of minimum, or most negative, growth acceleration after the inflection point.

Thus, \[\arg\max_{t<T_i} W''(t),\] and \[\arg\min_{t>T_i} W''(t).\]
These points describe the transition from increasing acceleration toward maximum growth rate and the subsequent period of strongest deceleration.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.4 Ontogenetic growth force
The ontogenetic growth force is defined as in Garcia-Neto et al. (2020):
\[W'(t)W''(t).\]
PGM may report:

\(F1\): maximum OGF before the inflection point;
\(F2\): the inflection-point location represented in the OGF sequence;

Because \(W'(t)\) is nonnegative for an increasing growth trajectory, the sign of OGF generally follows the sign of \(W''(t)\).
OGF-based points consider the magnitude of growth rate in the transition points from acceleration.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.5 Effective growth onset
Available onset descriptors may include:

\(Tan.\): tangent-based onset;
\(Thr.\): threshold-based onset;
\(PAA\): Acceleration-derived onset;
\(F0\): OGF-derived onset.


12.5.1 Tangent method
The tangent method uses the tangent line at the point of maximum growth rate and calculates its intersection with the baseline response represented by the fitted value at the beginning of the evaluated interval.
Its result depends on the observed or selected lower time boundary.


12.5.2 Threshold method
The threshold method identifies the first time at which the fitted trajectory reaches a selected proportion of its fitted late-stage value.
The result depends directly on the chosen threshold.


12.5.3 Absolute Acceleration Point
PAA is identified before \(P1\) from a zero crossing of the fourth derivative of the growth function (Korkmaz et al. 2018).
It represents a transition in the evolution of growth acceleration.


12.5.4 OGF-derived onset
The OGF-derived onset is calculated using the third derivative of the OGF before \(P1\).
It represents a transition in the evolution of the weighted growth acceleration.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.6 Late-growth descriptors
Available late-stage descriptors may include:

\(F3\): an OGF-derived late point;
\(PDA\): Point of Asymptotic Deceleration (Mischan et al. 2011).

These are identified after \(P2\) using derivative-based rules.
They indicate geometric transitions toward the late portion of the fitted trajectory. From that point, growth acceleration decreases very slowly, as it asymptotically approach zero (Mischan et al. 2011).

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.7 Integral descriptors
PGM may calculate the area under the curve (AUC) for the fitted growth function and its first derivative.
It may be useful to summarize growth “intensity” in a single metric across different trajectories (treatments, lineages, or other factors). Comparisons require the same time unit, response unit, interval, and fitted-variable definition.
The area under the fitted growth curve:
\[\int_{t_L}^{t_U} W(t),dt.\]
It may also calculate the integrated squared growth rate:
\[\int_{t_L}^{t_U}
\left[W'(t)\right]^2dt,\]
and the response-weighted integrated squared growth rate (Garcia-Neto et al. 2020):
\[\int_{t_L}^{t_U}
W(t)\left[W'(t)\right]^2dt.\]
If a custom integration interval is not provided, the AUC will be calculated for the complete time vector provided.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.8 Numerical evaluation
Critical points are located on a dense time grid spanning the fitted interval.
Consequently, their reported precision is affected by the numerical grid resolution and should not be interpreted as exact analytic precision.

title: 12  Critical Points
text:
12.9 Uncertainty
The current critical-point and integral tables provide point estimates.
Confidence intervals for derived times and integral descriptors are not automatically implied by confidence intervals for the model parameters.
Bootstrap, simulation, or delta-method procedures would be required to quantify their uncertainty separately.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
13.1 Estimation information
The Estimation Methods table summarizes the statistical and computational specification used for each model setup.
Depending on the selected options, it may report:
This table should be consulted before reporting a model because the same growth equation may be fitted under substantially different fixed, random, variance, and correlation assumptions.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
13  Model Evaluation
13  Model Evaluation
text:
13.3 Interpretation of p-values
The p-values reported in the parameter table are coefficient-level tests obtained on the model estimation scale.
They should not be interpreted as tests of the natural-scale parameter estimate itself.
Reference-profile rows do not receive a p-value.
For a categorical predictor, a coefficient tests the corresponding contrast against its reference level.
For an interaction, the p-value tests the associated interaction coefficient.
For factors or interactions represented by several coefficients, these values are not equivalent to an omnibus test of the entire term.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
13.4 Random Effects table
When an NLME model is fitted, PGM may display a separate Random Effects table.
The table reports:

grouping structure;
growth parameter;
estimated random-effect standard deviation on the natural parameter scale.

Within each grouping level, the current model uses a diagonal covariance structure; covariance or correlation among random growth parameters is therefore not reported.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
13  Model Evaluation
text:
13.6 Goodness-of-fit measures

13.6.1 Akaike information criterion
The Akaike information criterion is \[-2\ell + 2k,\]
where \(\ell\) is the maximized log-likelihood and \(k\) is the number of estimated parameters counted by the fitted likelihood.
Lower AIC values indicate better expected predictive information performance among comparable models.
The absolute AIC value is not interpreted independently.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
14.1 Bayesian information criterion
The Bayesian information criterion is \[-2\ell+k\log(n).\]
BIC generally penalizes model complexity more strongly than AIC as the sample size increases.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
14.2 Descriptive coefficient of determination
PGM calculates \[1-
\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}
{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}.\]
This is a descriptive residual-based statistic on the response scale.
For nonlinear mixed-effects models, it should not be described as the marginal or conditional \(R^2\) commonly defined specifically for mixed models.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
14.3 Adjusted descriptive coefficient of determination
PGM calculates an adjusted form based on residual degrees of freedom: \[1-
\frac{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-p)}
{\mathrm{SST}/(n-1)}.\]
Its interpretation remains descriptive.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
text:
14.4 Error metrics

14.4.1 Root mean squared error
\[\sqrt{
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_i
(y_i-\hat y_i)^2
}.\]
RMSE uses the response unit and is relatively sensitive to large residuals.


14.4.2 Relative RMSE
\[\frac{\mathrm{RMSE}}{\bar y}.\]
RRMSE is dimensionless but may behave poorly when the response mean is close to zero.


14.4.3 Mean absolute error
\[\frac{1}{n}
\sum_i
|y_i-\hat y_i|.\]


14.4.4 Median absolute error
\[\operatorname{median}
\left(
|y_i-\hat y_i|
\right).\]
MedAE is less sensitive to isolated large residuals than RMSE or MAE.


14.4.5 Symmetric mean absolute percentage error
PGM calculates \[\frac{100}{n}
\sum_i
\frac{2|y_i-\hat y_i|}
{|y_i|+|\hat y_i|}.\]
A small numerical safeguard is used when both the observed and fitted values are close to zero.

title: 13  Model Evaluation
14  Residual diagnostics
text:
14.1 Residuals versus fitted values
PGM provides a four-panel residual diagnostic display.
This plot is used to investigate:
A satisfactory pattern should be centered near zero without pronounced systematic structure.

title: 14  Residual diagnostics
14  Residual diagnostics
14  Residual diagnostics
text:
14.3 Normal Q–Q plot
The Q–Q plot compares the empirical residual distribution with the normal distribution.
Large systematic departures from the diagonal may indicate skewness, heavy tails, outliers, or model misspecification.
Minor departures should not be interpreted mechanically, particularly with large datasets.

title: 14  Residual diagnostics
text:
14.4 Residual autocorrelation
The autocorrelation plot assesses whether residuals remain associated across neighboring measurement occasions.
When Correlation Groups are supplied, the residual ACF is calculated within the grouping units defined by those variables.
When no explicit Correlation Groups are supplied for an NLME model, PGM uses the innermost random-effects grouping level for the diagnostic grouping.
Persistent residual autocorrelation may indicate that the selected mean structure, random effects, or residual correlation structure is insufficient.

title: 14  Residual diagnostics
text:
14.5 Residual scale
For generalized nonlinear and nonlinear mixed-effects models, PGM uses normalized residuals that account for the fitted variance and correlation structure.
For ordinary nonlinear least squares, raw residuals are standardized by the estimated residual standard deviation.

15.1 Chicken Growth — Aggrey (2002)

17.1 Citation

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
Unified growth-model family: Tjørve and Tjørve (Tjørve and Tjørve 2010; Tjørve and Tjørve 2017)
nonlinear least-squares estimation: minpack.lm (Elzhov et al. 2023)

title: 17  Academic Reporting
17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.3 Ordinary nonlinear model
A possible methods statement is:

Growth trajectories were fitted using the PGM module for jamovi. The [Richards] growth equation was estimated by nonlinear least squares, with initial optimization performed using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm. Model adequacy was evaluated using parameter estimates, information criteria, prediction-error measures, and residual diagnostics.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.4 Generalized nonlinear least squares
When a variance function is included:

Growth trajectories were fitted using the PGM module for jamovi. The [Richards] growth equation was estimated by nonlinear least squares, with initial optimization performed using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm. The resulting estimates were used to initialize a generalized nonlinear least-squares model with a [power/exponential/constant-plus-power] residual variance function based on the fitted response.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.5 Nonlinear mixed-effects model
For models containing random growth parameters, a possible methods statement is:

Growth trajectories were fitted using the PGM module for jamovi. The [Unified Richards/Gompertz/Logistic/von Bertalanffy] model was expressed using the [Ti/W0] parameterization. Fixed effects of [predictors] were assigned to [growth parameters], including the interaction between [predictors] where specified. Between-[subject/group] variation in [parameters] was represented using parameter-specific random effects, with [grouping hierarchy]. Models were estimated by maximum likelihood after initialization from a Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear fit.


17.5.1 Fixed effects and interactions
When parameter-specific predictors are fitted:

Systematic variation in the growth parameters was modeled using fixed effects. The parameter [A/K/Ti/W0/d] included effects of [predictors]. The interaction between [X] and [Z] was included to allow the effect of one predictor on the growth parameter to depend on the level of the other.

PGM reports coefficient-level p-values on the model estimation scale. For factors or interactions represented by several coefficients, these should not be described as omnibus tests unless an appropriate joint test has been performed separately.


17.5.2 Residual autocorrelation
When applicable:

Residual dependence within [Correlation Groups] was modeled using a first-order [AR(1)/CAR(1)] correlation structure.

For CAR(1):

Residual correlation was modeled as a function of the actual temporal distance between observations.



17.5.3 Heteroscedasticity
When applicable:

Residual variance was modeled as a [power/exponential/constant-plus-power] function of the absolute fitted response.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.6 Model comparison
A possible statement is:

Candidate specifications were compared using [AIC/AICc] and BIC, together with residual diagnostics and biological plausibility of the estimated parameters. Information criteria were compared only across models fitted to the same response observations.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.7 Derived growth descriptors
When reporting derivative-based descriptors:

Derived growth values and times were calculated from the fitted growth function and its derivatives, presented as point estimates. These quantities were treated as model-based geometric descriptors.

title: 17  Academic Reporting
17  Academic Reporting
text:
17.9 Figures

17.9.1 Growth-curve figures

observed data;
fitted trajectory;
response and time units;
group or subject definition;
critical-point labels, when used.



17.9.2 Residual figures
Residual figures should be reported or summarized whenever model assumptions are important to the conclusions.
